opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few different motivations at play, and they don't all have to line up for the system to be useful.

On the user side, there's a real appetite for this information that just isn't being met right now. I talk to a lot of developers, companies, and even procurement folks at universities and governments, and they're increasingly being asked about the environmental footprint of the tools they use. Many organizations have sustainability commitments, some have reporting obligations, and when they go to choose a model, they have almost nothing to go on. You can compare models on accuracy, latency, and price per token, but energy is a black box. So if you give people a simple, comparable signal, like a star rating, I think a lot of them will use it, the same way people glance at the Energy Star label when buying a fridge. It's not the only factor, but it becomes part of the decision.

For model providers, especially open-source developers, there's a reputational upside. If you've put real effort into making a model efficient, through distillation, quantization, or smarter architecture choices, you currently get very little credit for that. A rating gives you a way to show it off. We've already seen that with leaderboards: people love to be at the top of a leaderboard, and that competitive dynamic can push the whole field toward efficiency rather than just bigger and bigger models.

Then there's the regulatory angle. Things like the EU AI Act are starting to talk about energy reporting, and I think a lot of companies would rather engage with a voluntary, community-driven standard now than have something imposed on them later that they had no say in. Being early also lets you shape the methodology.

Now, will everyone participate? No, at least not at first. The big closed-model providers have been pretty reluctant to disclose energy numbers. But the original Energy Star program was voluntary too, and it became a de facto standard because consumers started expecting the label. If enough models are rated, the absence of a rating starts to say something. That's the dynamic I'm hoping for: once transparency becomes the norm, opting out becomes harder to justify.

r001.rationale: The response does not propose locally run evaluation code or say that it would let providers avoid disclosing company secrets.

r002.rationale: It says an efficiency rating could give providers reputational credit, and separately compares the label to Energy Star on a fridge. It does not connect providers’ motivation to the way appliance manufacturers seek Energy Star certification.

r003.rationale: The response says energy is a black box and organizations have almost nothing to go on when choosing models, identifying a lack of decision-support information that a comparable rating could address.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because voluntary is the key word there, right? Nobody's forcing anyone to do this. But I actually think there's a lot of pull from both sides, and that's why I'm optimistic about it.

So on the provider side, the way I see it is, right now there's this kind of race to the top in terms of capability, and everybody's benchmarking on the same leaderboards, and energy just isn't part of that conversation at all. And what we've seen with Energy Star for appliances, when it started back in the nineties, it was also voluntary, and manufacturers adopted it because it became a differentiator. You could put that little blue sticker on your fridge and people would pick your fridge. And I think with AI models, especially now that there are so many models that are roughly comparable in terms of performance, efficiency becomes a way to stand out. If I'm a smaller lab, or an open-source project, and I can say, look, my model does ninety-five percent of what the big model does at a tenth of the energy, that's a really compelling story. And it's also something that the big players can't easily buy their way out of, which I think makes it kind of interesting from a competitive standpoint.

And the other thing is, a lot of these companies have made public sustainability commitments. They have net zero targets, they have ESG reporting, and right now there's a lot of hand-waving around the AI part of that. So having an external, standardized rating gives them something concrete to point to. It's actually easier for them than having to invent their own methodology and then defend it.

On the user side, and by users I mean both developers picking a model off of a hub and enterprises making procurement decisions, there's a real information gap right now. People ask me all the time, which model should I use, and they genuinely want to factor in energy, but they have no way to compare. The numbers that providers publish, when they publish them at all, are measured in completely different ways, different hardware, different tasks. So the value of something like Energy Star is really the standardization. It's one methodology, same tasks, same measurement approach, and you get a score that actually means something across models. And I think once that exists, people will use it, because the demand is already there, the data just hasn't been.

And then honestly, the last piece is regulation. I think a lot of providers see something like this coming anyway. The EU AI Act already has provisions around reporting energy consumption for certain models. So if you engage with a voluntary system now, you kind of get to shape what the standard looks like, rather than having it imposed on you later. That's a pretty strong incentive for the people who are paying attention.

So, is everyone going to jump on board on day one? Probably not. But I think if you get a critical mass of models rated, especially open models where we can actually run the measurements ourselves, then it creates pressure on the ones who are holding out. Because at some point, not having a rating starts to look like you have something to hide.

r001.rationale: The response does not propose locally executed evaluation code or say that it would let providers protect company secrets.

r002.rationale: It says Energy Star adoption made appliance efficiency a differentiator and suggests model providers could stand out by earning ratings.

r003.rationale: It describes an information gap: users lack comparable energy data and a standardized way to compare models when choosing what to use.

astra-6.text:
I think there are incentives on both sides. For users, right now, it’s really hard to make an informed choice. You can compare models on performance, but you don’t necessarily know how much energy they use. A rating would make that visible, so you could say, “These two models both do what I need, but this one uses less energy.”

For providers, efficiency is something they can compete on, and lower energy use can also mean lower costs. If customers start asking for that information, there’s a reason to disclose it and improve. It doesn’t require everyone to make sustainability their top priority. It gives people a straightforward way to include it in their decisions. The challenge is making the rating credible and the comparisons meaningful.

r001.rationale: The response does not propose locally executed evaluation code or mention protecting providers’ company secrets.

r002.rationale: It mentions competition, costs, and customer demand, but not reputational appeal from green certification or the appliance Energy Star analogy.

r003.rationale: It says users cannot readily compare models’ energy use and therefore struggle to make informed choices; a rating would make efficiency visible for selection.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are different incentives on both sides. For users, right now, there’s very little visibility into the energy consumption of these models. Even if you want to make a more sustainable choice, you don’t necessarily have the information to do that. A rating would give you something accessible to compare, alongside things like performance and cost.

For model providers, it’s a way to differentiate themselves. If you’ve put work into making your model more efficient, you want to be able to communicate that. And my hope is that, as users start asking for that information, there’s an incentive for more providers to participate.

It’s not going to solve everything, and voluntary participation has limitations. But it gives us a starting point for making energy efficiency part of the conversation when people choose a model.

r001.rationale: The response does not propose locally executed evaluation code or address protecting company secrets.

r002.rationale: It says providers could differentiate themselves, but does not connect motivation to the reputational appeal of green certification or compare providers with appliance manufacturers.

r003.rationale: It says users have little visibility into model energy use and that a rating would make efficiency easier to compare when choosing a model.
